(2015) explicitly state in the Abstract, 'The Current Study,' and Discussion opening sentence that they genotyped only OXTR rs53576 and coded observed warmth, control, and negativity in 500 twin families to replicate and extend prior rs53576 parenting work (Bakermans-Kranenburg & van IJzendoorn, 2008, shipped row 9; Michalska et al., 2014, target 1). The primary abstract of Feldman et al. (2012, 10.1016/j.biopsych.2011.12.025; N=352) shows that Feldman et al. tested plasma oxytocin, CD38 rs3796863, and OXTR rs2254298 and rs1042778 with infant touch and gaze synchrony—not rs53576—and Klahr et al.'s Discussion explicitly notes that OXTR rs2254298 and rs1042778 were unmeasured and left for future research. Because the paper simultaneously defines its empirical hypothesis around rs53576 while characterizing its result as constructively replicating the broader OXTR-variant parenting link including Feldman et al. (2012), and the full body of Feldman et al. (2012) is unavailable locally, scope ambiguity between a variant-specific retest and a gene-level conceptual replication remains irreducible.

decisions.reason: Zimmermann and Lange (2022) designed Experiment 1 (N=6) to replicate the context dependency of perisaccadic displacement suppression reported by Zimmermann (2020, 10.7554/elife.49700, shipped row 2268) before testing contrast suppression in Experiment 2. In a 2x2 repeated-measures ANOVA on Experiment 1 displacement discrimination with factors stimulus time (baseline vs. perisaccadic) and session type (no context vs. context), the authors cite both Bridgeman, Hendry, and Stark (1975) and Zimmermann (2020) for the perisaccadic decline in displacement detection (stimulus time main effect F(1,5)=18.85, p=0.007) and Zimmermann (2020) for the session-type main effect and interaction. The complete primary XML of Zimmermann (2020) confirms that Zimmermann (2020) Experiment 1 already directly measured and statistically confirmed baseline perisaccadic vs. pre-saccadic displacement suppression in no-context sessions (t(3)=-9.38, p=0.0026, d=1.7, citing Bridgeman et al., 1975) alongside context sessions (t(3)=3.68, p=0.017) in the same experimental paradigm. Under the codebook closest-in-chain rule, Zimmermann (2020) is the immediate study in the empirical chain encompassing both the baseline perisaccadic displacement suppression and its context modulation, so the ancestral source Bridgeman et al. (1975) is not an omitted independent target.

Baumann (2018, N=60) uses standardized affective sounds (IADS) prior to neutral scene encoding under low vs. high category-exemplar interference to provide 'a conceptual replication of findings by Kensinger and colleagues (c.f. Kensinger, 2009a, b), showing that negative emotions specifically facilitate the encoding of perceptual details.' Shipped row 731 codes the review Kensinger (2009a, 10.1177/1754073908100432), which is under separate frozen field review (scope_primary_731_0005). In the Introduction, Baumann cites Kensinger, Garoff-Eaton, and Schacter (2007, 10.1162/jocn.2007.19.11.1872) as an example showing greater memory accuracy for visual details of negative vs. positive items, and Kensinger and Schacter (2006) as an example where visual input was matched across groups while emotional appraisal varied. Neither primary text is locally available, and Baumann's single experiment combines visual scene detail discrimination (as in 2007) with matched neutral visual stimuli across valence conditions (analogous to 2006) without citing either primary study in the Methods, Results, or Discussion. Because replacing shipped review row 731 with a primary original would not create an extra row unless multiple primary findings are independently targeted, and the source does not resolve whether 2007 is an additional target or the primary replacement for row 731, this candidate is undeterminable.

decisions.quote: an we feel good about equivalent gains. Loss aversion accounts for various anomalous choice behaviors, such as the endowment effect (15), [although see (18, 19)]. Also integral to Prospect Theory is the notion of diminishing sensitivity to both losses and gains from a reference point (17, 20), which, when it comes to risk preferences, predicts a pattern of choices whereby people tend to be risk averse for gains and risk seeking for losses. Consequently, reframing a given set of outcomes as relative gains versus relative losses changes people’s risk preferences over that set. So far, loss aversion and diminishing sensitivity have been observed for various tangible outcomes, including nonconsumer outcomes such as human lives (21, 22), and a few nontangible resources, such as time (23–26), but not for information.The current research is closest to a set of studies in information science conducted by Rafaeli and Raban (27, 28), who replicated the endowment effect for information in a game mimicking sales decisions. decisions.reason: Litovsky et al. (2022) state in the Introduction that their research 'is closest to a set of studies in information science conducted by Rafaeli and Raban (27, 28), who replicated the endowment effect for information in a game mimicking sales decisions' (observing WTA > WTP in a computerized lemonade-stand trading task; verified in Rafaeli & Raban, 2003, JAIS, N=31/29 retained, and a linked 2003 conference paper, N=55) and state 'We extend their work in several critical ways' by eliminating elicitation/risk-aversion, monetary loss-aversion, and instrumental-profit confounds. In Study 2 (N=146), Litovsky et al. randomly endow half of participants with prospective ownership of a 3-fact noninstrumental trivia bundle before offering a choice between the 3-fact and 4-fact bundles, finding greater retention of the 3-fact bundle among endowed participants (68% vs. 46%, chi2(1, n=146)=7.03, P=0.008). However, Study 2 and the Discussion never cite Rafaeli and Raban (2003). Whether Study 2 serves as a de-confounded conceptual replication of Rafaeli and Raban's (2003) information-endowment finding or a distinct test of Prospect Theory loss aversion for noninstrumental facts is genuinely ambiguous in the source text.

decisions.quote: bserved greater willingness-to-accept prices than willingness-to-pay amounts. We extend their work in several critical ways. First, due to features of their elicitation method, Rafaeli and Raban attributed the endowment effect that they observed to risk aversion rather than loss aversion. Second, their observed preferences over information may be confounded by attitudes toward gaining and losing money, since their willingness-to-pay measure involved giving up money (which, due to loss aversion, people are reluctant to do), while their willingness-to-accept measure involved obtaining money. To avoid this issue, the studies reported herein do not involve money, but rather choices between different sets of information. Third, because the game they used was a novel task, there is significant uncertainty about the usefulness of the information involved. If that information was perceived to directly translate into financial rewards, it is impossible to determine whether the observed effect reflected loss aversion for information per se or for the in-game profits. To avoid this concern, our
decisions.reason: Litovsky et al. (2022) jointly cite Rafaeli and Raban (2003, ref. 27) and Raban and Rafaeli (2006, JASIST 57, 321-329, ref. 28) as the closest prior studies demonstrating an information endowment effect (WTA > WTP in a sales-decision game) that their nonmonetary, noninstrumental paradigm extends. The recovered author abstract for Raban and Rafaeli (2006, N=294) confirms that it also measured the WTA > WTP endowment gap in the business simulation game while adding manipulations of information source nature (human expertise vs. plain information) and status (original vs. copy). However, the full text of Raban and Rafaeli (2006) is unavailable, preventing verification of the exact empirical finding chain and sample relationship between the 2003 and 2006 reports, and Litovsky et al. Study 2 (N=146) does not manipulate source expertise or copy status. Combined with the unresolved conceptual-scope ambiguity of whether Study 2's bundle-retention test retests the cited WTA/WTP trading studies or only extends general endowment theory to noninstrumental facts, whether Raban and Rafaeli (2006) is a genuine target or superseded/distinct in the chain is undeterminable.
